So I've come up with a couple theories from the trailer.

At 3:27, Zero says "so the Major sought a system that used information - words - to control the subconscious."

I want to highlight the idea of controlling the subconscious. I think that is major here. I think that the things we see in the beginning, and near the end, with BB walking down a blood-stained hallway and then seeming quite insane lying in the pile of dead bodies around his comrades, shows us that BB is being influenced using language on a subconscious level. I think Zero is using something to influence him.

I think this is a major reason that he is seeing Skullface seemingly in his own mind, too. I also noticed that the part of Skullface's face covered by the mask is roughly the same as the part of Quiet's face that becomes black when she goes into a kind of fighting mode.

Maybe Quiet and Skullface are connected. Maybe Quiet is to be used to carry a message to Big Boss subconsciously and Skullface is a means to communicate these thoughts, but only within his mind, in a way that BB will think it's coming from an actual person.

From wikipedia:

There are suggestions that the negative consequences of trans fat consumption go beyond the cardiovascular risk. In general, there is much less scientific consensus asserting that eating trans fat specifically increases the risk of other chronic health problems:

Alzheimer's Disease: A study published in Archives of Neurology in February 2003 suggested that the intake of both trans fats and saturated fats promote the development of Alzheimer disease,[78] although not confirmed in an animal model.[79] It has been found that trans fats impaired memory and learning in middle-age rats. The rats' brains of trans-fat eaters had fewer proteins critical to healthy neurological function. Inflammation in and around the hippocampus, the part of the brain responsible for learning and memory. These are the exact types of changes normally seen at the onset of Alzheimer's, but seen after six weeks, even though the rats were still young.[80]

Cancer: There is no scientific consensus that consumption of trans fats significantly increases cancer risks across the board.[67] The American Cancer Society states that a relationship between trans fats and cancer "has not been determined."[81] One study has found a positive connection between trans fat and prostate cancer.[82] However, a larger study found a correlation between trans fats and a significant decrease in high-grade prostate cancer.[83] An increased intake of trans fatty acids may raise the risk of breast cancer by 75%, suggest the results from the French part of the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition.[84][85]

Diabetes: There is a growing concern that the risk of type 2 diabetes increases with trans fat consumption.[67] However, consensus has not been reached.[53] For example, one study found that risk is higher for those in the highest quartile of trans fat consumption.[86] Another study has found no diabetes risk once other factors such as total fat intake and BMI were accounted for.[87]

Obesity: Research indicates that trans fat may increase weight gain and abdominal fat, despite a similar caloric intake.[88] A 6-year experiment revealed that monkeys fed a trans fat diet gained 7.2% of their body weight, as compared to 1.8% for monkeys on a mono-unsaturated fat diet.[89][90] Although obesity is frequently linked to trans fat in the popular media,[91] this is generally in the context of eating too many calories; there is not a strong scientific consensus connecting trans fat and obesity, although the 6-year experiment did find such a link, concluding that "under controlled feeding conditions, long-term TFA consumption was an independent factor in weight gain. TFAs enhanced intra-abdominal deposition of fat, even in the absence of caloric excess, and were associated with insulin resistance, with evidence that there is impaired post-insulin receptor binding signal transduction."[90]

Liver Dysfunction: Trans fats are metabolized differently by the liver than other fats and interfere with delta 6 desaturase. Delta 6 desaturase is an enzyme involved in converting essential fatty acids to arachidonic acid and prostaglandins, both of which are important to the functioning of cells.[92]

Infertility in women: One 2007 study found, "Each 2% increase in the intake of energy from trans unsaturated fats, as opposed to that from carbohydrates, was associated with a 73% greater risk of ovulatory infertility...".[93]

Major depressive disorder: Spanish researchers analysed the diets of 12,059 people over six years and found those who ate the most trans fats had a 48 per cent higher risk of depression than those who did not eat trans fats.[94] One mechanism may be trans-fats' substitution for docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) levels in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC). Very high intake of trans-fatty acids (43% of total fat) in mice from 2 to 16 months of age was associated with lowered DHA levels in the brain (p=0.001) [95] When the brains of 15 major depressive subjects who had committed suicide were examined post-mortem and compared against 27 age-matched controls, the suicidal brains were found to have 16% less (male average) to 32% (female average) less DHA in the OFC. The OFC controls reward, reward expectation, and empathy (all of which are reduced in depressive mood disorders) and regulates the limbic system.[96]

Behavioral irritability and aggression: a 2012 observational analysis of subjects of an earlier study found a strong relation between dietary trans fat acids and self-reported behavioral aggression and irritability, suggesting but not establishing causality.[97]
